title: Observability and Path Health
html:
“Did it go through?” You have probably asked that yourself, after a bank transfer, a booking, or a payment page that stopped responding before it showed a confirmation. The bank may have committed the transfer while the app lost the response. To settle what happened, the records at the customer interface, API, and authoritative database have to be examined together.

A Baodium customer contacted support after a payment page continued loading and a refresh showed the order as pending. A confirmation email arrived later, but the customer worried that refreshing the page might have created another purchase. Support found one order. Payment Service logs showed two authorization attempts, while the gateway and browser records did not establish which result the customer had seen.

The service dashboards showed healthy CPU and memory, yet the provider had become slower and connection acquisition had increased. Those measurements explained part of the delay. They could not connect the customer’s browser action, the committed order, the provider attempts, and the response sent by the gateway. The engineers needed a way to reconstruct that sequence for one operation.

The term observability comes from control theory, where it refers to inferring internal state from measurements.1 In software, we need enough evidence to reconstruct what happened to an operation. For Baodium, the database could confirm that an order committed, the gateway could record the response it sent, and the browser could report what appeared to the customer. We will call each location an observation boundary, because its records establish a different part of the outcome.

Request Observation Boundaries

When you place an order online, several systems are involved, and each one can record only its own part of what happened. The database can record that the order was committed, the gateway can record that it finished sending a response, and only the browser can record that the customer saw a confirmation. No one of these records guarantees that the next event occurred. An order can be committed while its response is lost on the way back, and a response can reach a browser after the customer has already left the page. You need all three observations, and you should treat any missing record as an unknown outcome rather than a success.

At the database, every change to an order or payment state also writes a row to a state-transition table in the same transaction. If the transaction rolls back, the row rolls back with it, so any total calculated from these rows matches what was committed. A counter incremented in application code after the commit cannot offer that guarantee, because the process could crash between the commit and the increment.

The gateway is the reverse proxy in front of every Baodium service, and it writes one access-log entry for each request when that request ends. Because every request passes through the gateway, the log also captures requests whose backend crashed and requests that the customer abandoned. Nginx, for example, logs status 499 when the client closes the connection before the response is sent, and the checkout gateway records those requests with a disconnected outcome. Each entry also records the route, HTTP status, duration, request identifier, and a protected reference to the operation, which we will examine later in the chapter.

In the browser, a short script sends a submission report when the customer places the order and a display report when a result appears on screen. Both reports include timestamps from the browser’s Performance API and are sent with navigator.sendBeacon, which asks the browser to deliver the report even if the page is closing. Delivery is still not guaranteed, because ad blockers, privacy settings, crashed tabs, and network failures all stop some reports from arriving. A checkout without a display report is treated as unknown rather than successful.

The gateway entry also defines a request’s server-side duration, which runs from the moment the gateway accepts an authenticated, well-formed request until it finishes the response or records that the request ended without one. Connection setup, TLS negotiation, and page rendering fall outside that interval, so they are visible only in the browser’s timing, as Figure Figure shows.

With all three records in place, comparing them shows where a checkout went wrong. A committed order paired with gateway status 499 shows that the client disconnected before the gateway finished sending its response, although the gateway cannot tell you what the browser displayed. A gateway response reporting a pending outcome, paired with a display report that still shows an indefinite progress indicator, points to a separate problem in the page itself.

Metrics, Logs, and Distributed Traces

During a checkout incident, the team needs three kinds of evidence. Metrics reveal changes in request rates, latency, errors, and resource usage across many requests. A log records an individual event, such as a rejected authorization or a failed provider call. A distributed trace connects timed operations across the services that processed one request.

These records have different limits. A counter can summarize millions of requests without retaining each request’s details, but its labels must be bounded to avoid excessive time-series cardinality. Logs retain event details at a cost proportional to volume. Traces expose per-request timing, although sampling may exclude the request being investigated. Instrumentation or collection failures can also leave gaps in any of these records.

At Baodium, metrics identified the affected request path. Traces then located the database wait or provider call responsible for the delay. Logs and durable operation records established what happened after checkout had stopped waiting. The distinction matters whenever an asynchronous operation continues beyond the original HTTP request.

Telemetry Collection and Storage

Between the line of code that records a measurement and the graph an engineer opens during an incident, telemetry passes through several layers. Most organizations have the same layers, whatever tools they use: instrumentation inside each service, collectors near each workload, a processing tier that filters, samples, and buffers data, a storage system for each kind of telemetry, and dashboards and alerting on top. At Baodium, the instrumentation is the OpenTelemetry SDK in every service, and collection is handled by an OpenTelemetry Collector agent on every host, together with Prometheus scraping for metrics. Processing happens in a pool of gateway collectors. Prometheus and Thanos store metrics, Loki stores logs, Tempo stores traces, and Grafana and Alertmanager provide dashboards and alerts. Three design decisions in this pipeline affect everything else in the chapter.

The first decision is how metrics travel from each service to the store. With the pull model, a scraper such as Prometheus fetches each service’s /metrics endpoint on a fixed schedule, every 15 seconds at Baodium. With the push model, each service sends its data to a collector on its own schedule. The two models fail in different ways. If Prometheus cannot reach a service, it records a failed scrape, and you can alert on that failure. If a service that pushes its metrics fails, however, its data stops arriving, and on a dashboard that silence is indistinguishable from a healthy service with nothing to report. That is why the platform team pulls its metrics. Traces and logs are pushed, but only as far as an agent collector on the same host. The SDK sends data to that agent in the background, so a slow or unavailable telemetry backend never delays a customer’s request.

The second decision is where to apply the rules that every service must obey. Baodium’s agents forward all telemetry to a central pool of gateway collectors, which remove known sensitive fields, add resource attributes, sample traces, and buffer data when a backend slows down. If each team implemented these rules in its own service, some services would leave them out and others would run outdated versions. A central tier makes the rules consistent, but it also creates a shared dependency, because a failure in the gateway pool affects the telemetry of every service.

The third decision is how to link the separate stores. Metrics, logs, and spans end up in three different systems, so engineers need shared keys to go from one to another. OpenTelemetry attaches resource attributes, such as service.name, service.version, and the deployment region, to everything a service emits. Trace identifiers in log records connect logs to traces, and exemplars, which you will meet later in the chapter, connect histogram buckets to traces. With these keys in place, an engineer can select a slow point on a latency graph, open the trace behind it, and then read the logs written during that trace.

Monitoring Coverage and Failure Signals

When failures increase, the first thing to rule out is the obvious. Is every required service reachable, and are its instances running? Baodium runs about forty services, each deployed as several instances, and every service has the same five kinds of monitoring.

Health endpoints.

Chapter 6 described Kubernetes liveness and readiness probes and why both should check only the instance itself. Those probes make Kubernetes restart a stuck container or stop sending it traffic, but they do not alert anyone, so the other four kinds of monitoring exist to tell people what is happening.

Scrape status and inventory.

Baodium’s instance alerts come from Prometheus. For each instance it scrapes, Prometheus records a metric called up, which is 1 when the scrape succeeds and 0 when it fails, and an alert on up == 0 that lasts two minutes detects an instance that has stopped responding. An instance that drops out of service discovery, however, is no longer scraped at all, so its up series ends instead of falling to 0, and the alert has nothing to evaluate. Baodium closes this gap with three more checks. An absent(up{job="order-service"}) rule fires when a critical service has no up series at all. A comparison between the number of scraped instances and the kube_deployment_status_replicas_available metric from kube-state-metrics detects instances that are running but not being scraped. And a job that compares the service catalog with Prometheus’s targets every five minutes detects services that were never discovered in the first place.

Request metrics.

An instance can respond to every scrape and still fail every request it serves. Every service also exports the same three request metrics, known as RED: request rate, errors, and duration. Together they describe what a caller experiences, which is how much processing arrives, how much of it fails, and how long it takes, and because every service uses the same metric names, one dashboard template covers all forty services. For resources such as connection pools and worker pools, a companion set called USE looks at utilization, saturation, and errors. Saturation is the one teams most often forget. For a connection pool, it is the number of requests waiting to acquire a connection, the measurement that revealed the problem in Chapter 1.

External probes.

All of the checks so far run inside Baodium’s network, so they cannot detect a failure that happens in front of it. If DNS stops resolving, a certificate expires, or the content delivery network fails, customers cannot reach checkout at all, while the services behind it see only a drop in traffic and report no errors. To catch failures of this kind, the platform team simulates customers from outside its network. Synthetic probes run every minute from three locations in different regions, so that a network problem near one location is not mistaken for an outage. Some probes fetch the checkout page and verify its status code and certificate expiry date, some place a test order with a test card, and one looks up the status of a known test order.

Heartbeats.

Background workers need a check of their own, because they serve no requests and produce no request metrics. A worker that is stuck in a loop or waiting on a lock also goes on passing its liveness check. A healthy worker, however, always makes progress, so you measure progress. Each worker records the time of its last successful run in a gauge, which is a metric that can go down as well as up, and an alert fires when time() - reconciliation_last_success_timestamp_seconds exceeds ten minutes.

Not every one of these alerts should page an engineer. When a single instance fails, the load balancer sends its traffic to the surviving instances and customers are unaffected, so that alert goes to a ticket queue instead. During the incident, all five kinds of checks passed, which ruled out a failed service and led the engineer to the measurements of checkout itself.

Request Metrics and Latency Distributions

The team then checked whether the problem affected a single request or many. The checkout dashboard does this with two metrics emitted by the gateway, shown in Listing Listing: a counter, which only increases and records the number of requests, and a histogram, which records how long those requests took.

Labels and Cardinality

The names in braces are labels. They let the engineers examine checkout requests by route, region, application version, and outcome. Without them, a request counter combines the entire fleet into one total. A failure affecting a new version or one region can therefore be difficult to distinguish from healthy traffic elsewhere. With those labels, the team can compare the affected requests with the requests that completed normally.2

The outcome label needs a closer look, because each of its five values means something different. confirmed, rejected (for a business reason such as a payment decline), pending, failed, and disconnected. Together they reveal two common failures that average response time and HTTP error rates both miss, because neither failure produces an HTTP error. In the first, checkout responds within its target while a rising share of customers receive pending results instead of confirmations, which can even lower the average response time, since a pending response returns sooner than a confirmation. In the second, checkout confirms every order while customers wait well beyond the response target. Next to these panels, the dashboard shows the number of unresolved payment operations and the age of the oldest one, because a worker’s heartbeat shows only that reconciliation is running, not whether it is completing work as fast as it arrives, as Chapter 3 described.

Labels have a direct cost in storage and memory. Each distinct combination of label values becomes its own time series, and the monitoring system maintains an index entry and an in-memory buffer for every series. Cost scales with the number of combinations rather than with traffic, which is why each label must have a small, fixed set of values. This property is called cardinality. A route label containing the template /orders/{order_id} has one value however many orders exist, whereas a route label containing the literal path /orders/ creates a new series for every order until the monitoring system runs out of memory. Order numbers and similar identifiers belong in logs and traces instead, because those systems are built to look up individual records.

To see how fast the combinations multiply, suppose you added an instance label. Six regions, three versions, forty instances, and five outcomes produce 3,600 combinations. A classic Prometheus histogram with eight bucket limits stores eleven series for each combination, which are nine bucket series, including the implicit +Inf bucket, plus a sum and a total, so a single latency metric reaches 39,600 series. Baodium limits checkout metrics to four labels and opens per-instance views only after those labels have narrowed down the problem. Newer Prometheus versions also support native histograms, which store a whole distribution in a single series and reduce this cost considerably.

Latency Histograms

A single latency figure hides what an engineer most needs to know, which is how many users had a slow experience and how slow it was. An average blends the fast majority with the slow minority, so a small group of very slow requests barely changes it. If you have ever been told that the average wait at a clinic is ten minutes and then waited an hour, you know the problem. Percentiles avoid it because they describe how the whole distribution is spread out rather than only its center. The median is the latency at or below which half of all requests fall, and the 99th percentile is the latency at or below which about 99 percent fall, which makes it a measure of the slowest 1 percent. During the incident, the median checkout latency in the affected region was still about 0.8 seconds, while the 99th percentile rose from about 2 seconds to about 6.5 seconds. That pattern told the engineer that the problem was hurting a small share of requests badly rather than slowing every request a little.

You might expect each service instance to report its own 99th percentile, but percentiles cannot be combined across instances. If one instance reports 1 second and another reports 5 seconds, the fleet’s 99th percentile could fall almost anywhere between them, depending on how many requests each instance handled. Totals, by contrast, can be added. A histogram takes advantage of that by recording latency as a set of counters called buckets, each recording how many requests finished within a given upper limit, and the percentile is calculated from the bucket totals summed across all instances.

The checkout histogram uses limits of 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5, and 10 seconds. Because the 3-second limit matches the response target, the fraction of checkouts completed within target is an exact division of two counters rather than an estimate, as Listing Listing shows. In this and later PromQL listings, rate(…[5m]) converts each counter, which only ever increases, into a per-second rate over the last five minutes, and le="3" selects the 3-second bucket.

Any other percentile is an estimate, because the query engine interpolates within the bucket that contains it. Listing Listing sums the bucket totals across instances before estimating the percentile, which is the correct order of operations. Also show the number of requests next to every percentile, because a 99th percentile calculated from forty requests jumps whenever a single request is slow.

The estimated percentile depends on bucket boundaries.3

Because a histogram records a request only when it finishes, a request that hangs is invisible until it times out. Two gauges cover this gap by tracking the number of checkout requests in progress and the age of the oldest one.

Distributed Tracing and Latency Diagnosis

The metrics had narrowed the problem to the slowest checkouts in one region. Because a metric combines many requests into one number, however, it reports totals, and seeing where a single request spent its time takes a trace. A distributed trace can, because it records the path of one request through every service it touches. A trace resembles the timing sheet for a relay race, in which every leg is timed and the legs together account for the whole race. Each leg is a span, which is a named operation with a start time, an end time, a parent, and attributes such as an attempt number. Unlike a leg in a relay race, though, a span can contain smaller spans. Each service sends its spans to a shared backend, which reassembles them into a tree using the trace identifier and parent identifier that every span carries.

The engineer reached a slow trace from the latency graph through an exemplar. When a metrics library records a request’s duration while a trace is active, it can attach that trace’s identifier to the histogram bucket the request falls into, so a point on the 99th-percentile graph links directly to an actual request. Because the exemplar is attached before the sampling decision described later in the chapter, the trace it links to may have been discarded, in which case the engineer opens another exemplar from the same bucket.

A trace is useful only if its spans separate the operations that matter. If a single span called database.lookup covers waiting for a connection, running the SQL, and fetching rows, a slow lookup tells you nothing about which step was slow. The checkout path has a separate span for each kind of delay. Waiting for a database connection, using that connection, running each statement, each payment attempt, and each retry delay all appear as their own spans. These correspond to the three intervals Chapter 1 recorded as metrics. Instrumentation libraries create most of the spans automatically, but the two connection spans usually have to be added by hand, as in Listing Listing, because database instrumentation starts its span only when a statement is sent and cannot see the application’s connection pool.

The first block measures how long pool.acquire waits for a free connection. The second runs from the moment the connection is handed over until it is released, so every operation performed in between, including calls to other services, appears as a child of that span. When you read spans like these, remember that an outbound HTTP span measures the call from the caller’s side, including connection setup and network transfer. A long client span tells you that the call was slow as Payment Service observed it, but blaming the provider requires the provider’s own timings or a comparison with other callers.

Connection Pool Wait and Occupancy

Figure Figure shows the trace the engineer opened, with illustrative durations. It came from another customer’s checkout that completed normally, and its gateway span lasted 5.2 seconds. The request spent its first 1.8 seconds in db.connection.acquire. Once it had a connection, Order Service committed the acceptance record and called Payment Service while the connection was still assigned to it. The first authorization attempt timed out after 1.5 seconds, the retry policy waited 0.2 seconds, and a second attempt with the same idempotency key succeeded after 1.4 seconds. Recording the result, local processing, and sending the response took the final 0.3 seconds. Because Order Service released the connection just before responding, the connection span ends shortly before the gateway span.

This trace explained the empty slow-query log. Nearly all of the database-related time was spent in db.connection.acquire, before any statement ran, and a slow-query log records only statements that take a long time to execute. It is the same pattern Chapter 1 described, where requests lost their time waiting for a connection rather than inside the database.

The Payment Service call nested inside the connection span suggested a cause, but it did not prove one, because connections could also have been occupied by slow queries or by other requests sharing the pool. To tell these explanations apart, the engineer compared the pool’s connection occupancy with query duration and with provider latency. If slow queries had been responsible, occupancy would have risen with query duration. Instead, it rose and fell with provider latency. Together with the trace, this comparison established the mechanism. Each checkout occupied its database connection for the entire payment call, so when the provider slowed down, connections were busy for longer, and new checkouts had to wait for one at the start of their own requests. Chapter 3 had made Payment Service release its own connection before calling the provider, but Order Service’s checkout handler still occupied its connection while it waited for Payment Service. The same mistake had survived one service further upstream.

Span Timing and Critical-Path Analysis

A common mistake when reading a trace is to add up the span durations, which includes some time more than once whenever spans are nested. In this trace, the connection span contains the Payment Service call, which in turn contains both provider attempts and the retry delay, so adding them all up includes some of that time three times. Parallel branches cause a similar error, because two operations that run at the same time can add up to more than the time the caller waited. A simple check catches both mistakes. If the span durations add up to more than the request’s total duration, some of the spans overlap.

The critical path is the chain of operations that decides the end-to-end duration of the request. Think of cooking a meal in which the roast takes two hours and the vegetables take twenty minutes. Chopping the vegetables faster does not get dinner on the table any sooner. Speeding up work outside the critical path may reduce resource use, but it does not shorten the request unless the critical path changes. In this trace, the critical path ran through the connection wait, the first attempt, the retry delay, and the second attempt, which is why the changes discussed later in the chapter target the connection wait and the retry. When a trace shows a gap between spans, the request may have been waiting for a thread, running code that has no spans, or short of CPU, and a CPU profile of the service usually shows which. Timestamps from different hosts also need care, because a clock difference between machines can place a child span’s start before its parent’s.

OpenTelemetry Instrumentation

The preceding trace examples depend on instrumentation that creates those spans. The platform team produces them, along with its metrics and logs, using OpenTelemetry, an open standard divided into parts so that a library can be instrumented once and its telemetry sent to any backend. Application code calls the API, which does nothing until an SDK is installed. This separation lets library authors add instrumentation without forcing a particular backend on the applications that use their libraries. The SDK, configured when the service starts, samples, batches, and exports the data, and instrumentation libraries create spans automatically for common frameworks, such as HTTP servers and clients, gRPC, database drivers, and message queues.

Instrumentation libraries cover the frameworks they support, but they cannot capture business meaning, such as what a pending checkout is or why a payment attempt number matters. Teams add those spans and attributes by hand and agree on shared attribute names, such as checkout.outcome, payment.attempt, and operation_ref. For standard concepts, use the names that OpenTelemetry’s semantic conventions already define, such as http.response.status_code, so that dashboards and queries work the same way across services. Without that agreement, the same fact would be recorded under several names, and every query would have to account for all of them.

Trace Context Propagation

For a trace to track a request across services, each call has to pass along the trace it belongs to and the span that made the call. OpenTelemetry uses the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) Trace Context standard for this, which puts both values in a single header, shown in Listing Listing.

Reading from left to right, the header contains the format version (00), the 32-character trace identifier, the 16-character identifier of the calling span, and a flags field, in which 01 means that the caller sampled the trace. Client instrumentation injects this header into each outgoing request, and server instrumentation extracts it and makes the new span a child of the caller’s span.

Standard HTTP and gRPC libraries handle this automatically. When context is lost, the cause is usually either a hand-written client that never adds the header or a handoff to another thread. OpenTelemetry stores the active span in a context tied to the current thread or task, and a thread pool does not copy that context to its workers unless it is told to. In Python, for example, asyncio.to_thread copies the context, whereas a bare ThreadPoolExecutor does not. In the tracing backend, the symptom is a trace that ends abruptly, and then an unrelated trace that begins where the first one stopped.

Messages carry context in their headers in the same way, but a consumer usually should not continue the producer’s trace. A reconciliation job that runs minutes after checkout would otherwise stretch the checkout trace from seconds to minutes. Instead, the consumer starts a new trace and adds a span link back to the producer’s span.

At the edge of the system, a traceparent header from a public client is untrusted input. Accepting it would let any client choose its own trace identifiers or force every request to be recorded, and the companion baggage header would let it insert arbitrary data into internal telemetry. Baodium’s gateway discards both headers on public requests and starts a new trace.

Correlating Requests and Operations

For the customer, placing the order was one action. Across the service boundary, it was a series of separate executions. There was the original submission, then the refresh, and, for a checkout that ends in a pending state, a reconciliation job that may run minutes later. Each execution has its own trace, so tracing the whole user journey needs identifiers at three levels. A request identifier names a single HTTP request, so a refresh or a status poll gets a new one. A trace identifier groups the spans of one execution. An operation identifier groups every attempt and recovery step that belongs to one business operation, such as one checkout or one payment authorization.

Only the operation identifier covers the whole journey, so it must exist before the first request is sent. The platform team generates it when the checkout page is rendered and places it in a hidden form field. When the customer refreshed the page, the browser resubmitted the same value in request B that it had sent in request A. Order Service stores the identifier with the acceptance record, Payment Service passes it to the provider as the idempotency key, as designed in Chapter 3, and in telemetry it appears only in a protected form, operation_ref, which the end of this section explains.

The same identifiers link browser reports to gateway records, with one complication. Because a refresh resubmits the same operation, the operation reference cannot pair a display report with a single request, and because browser and server clocks can be several seconds apart, timestamps cannot pair them reliably either. To solve this, the gateway adds its request identifier to every response in a Server-Timing header, which the page’s script reads through the Performance API and includes in the display report. Each display report then matches a single gateway entry, and browser coverage can be measured as the share of completed checkout responses that have a matching display report.

Logs tie these separate traces together, because one log record can carry all three identifiers. Writing logs as structured JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) makes every field searchable, and OpenTelemetry’s logging integrations add the active trace and span identifiers automatically. Listing Listing shows the record for one payment attempt, in which retry_owner names the component that decides whether to retry, as Chapter 4 recommended.

Records like this are useful long after they are written when event names are fixed strings that a query can find in every release, and when outcomes tell a timeout apart from a decline or an unavailable connection. Most importantly, an outcome should describe only the attempt that produced it. A timeout means that Payment Service stopped waiting, not that the provider did nothing, and in this incident that distinction decided the outcome of the investigation.

Incident Reconstruction

When the engineer searched the logs for the order’s operation_ref, the records from both of the customer’s requests came back together. Sorting them by timestamp produced the timeline in Table Table, where op-1 stands for the customer’s operation.

The timeline shows three things. First, the gateway’s duration and the services’ durations have to be read separately. Request A’s gateway span ends at 4.5 seconds with a disconnected outcome, yet its service spans continue until 5.0 seconds, because the services learned that the browser had gone only when Order Service tried to write its response. Second, the refresh did not create a second order, because Order Service matched request B’s operation identifier to the operation it had accepted at 2.1 seconds. Third, the customer never saw a confirmation, because none was ever returned to them.

Whether the card had been charged twice could not be settled from Baodium’s records alone. The payment record showed one authorization, but it contained only what Payment Service had learned, and because attempt 1 had timed out, the provider might have authorized the card without Baodium ever receiving the response. That evidence had to come from the provider, which treats requests with the same idempotency key as one operation for 24 hours. The provider had marked its response to attempt 2 as a replay of an existing authorization, which meant that attempt 1 had succeeded and only its response had been lost, and a lookup through the provider’s API with the same key returned a single authorization. This is the reconciliation Chapter 3 described, now seen from the investigator’s side.

The confirmation email went through the transactional outbox from Chapter 3, so the email could not be sent for an order that was never confirmed, and the email consumer discarded the duplicate that a restarted relay could produce.

Sensitive Data in Telemetry

Logs are read by many people and retained for weeks, so they should never contain addresses, card details, credentials, or request bodies, and any identifier that someone could guess needs protection. For this reason, the operation identifier appears in telemetry only as operation_ref, a hash-based message authentication code (HMAC) computed with SHA-256 over the identifier keyed with a secret from a key-management service. A plain SHA-256 hash would not protect it, because operation identifiers use a predictable format, and anyone could hash every plausible value and compare the results. Because the key prevents that attack, only four components have access to it, the gateway plugin, the browser-report endpoint, Order Service, and the support lookup tool. Order Service passes the reference downstream with the trace context, so other services can log it without ever seeing the key. The key is rotated yearly, and the support tool retains the previous key for the 14 days that logs are searchable. Outside the checkout form and the services that handle the operation, the raw identifier is stored only in the operational database and sent only to the payment provider.

No single control can exclude all sensitive data from telemetry, so Baodium layers several. Services log through typed event structures that accept only approved fields, which prevents most mistakes at the source. The collectors remove deny-listed attributes and scan for patterns such as card numbers, although pattern matching misses values buried in JSON strings or exception messages. Access controls and short retention limit the damage when something does get through. Finally, a weekly test injects fake card numbers into staging requests and searches every backend for them, which shows whether the filters work.

Telemetry Sampling and Storage

Every layer of the pipeline uses CPU, network bandwidth, or storage. Because each kind of telemetry increases for a different reason, each needs its own controls.

Metrics.

Metric cost scales with the number of series, so the label rules described earlier provide most of the control. In addition, the gateway collectors drop any metric that no dashboard or alert uses, because instrumentation libraries often emit dozens of metrics that no engineer ever queries. Recording rules calculate expensive queries on a schedule and store the results as much smaller series, so a dashboard that shows the per-region 99th percentile reads a few precalculated series instead of thousands of raw ones. For older data, Thanos retains raw samples for 15 days and then downsamples them to five-minute and one-hour resolution, which is still adequate for 30-day indicators.

Logs.

Logs are often the largest telemetry cost, because every event produces a record, and the cheapest record is the one that is never written. At Baodium, load-balancer health checks every few seconds across hundreds of instances were producing millions of access-log lines a day that no engineer read, so successful health checks are now left out of the logs. Debug logging is disabled in production, informational messages written on every request are sampled, and warnings, errors, and business events such as payment attempts are always written. Logs are searchable for 14 days and are then archived to object storage, where a year of retention costs little but searches are slow.

Traces.

At its peak of 500 requests per second, with about 12 spans per request, checkout produces 6,000 spans per second. At roughly 1 KB per span, a full day at that rate would produce about 500 GB. The actual daily average is closer to 200 requests per second, or about 200 GB a day, so the collectors are sized for the peak while storage costs track the average.

Sampling reduces telemetry volume, but it can discard the traces needed after an incident. With head sampling, the first service’s SDK decides which traces to retain before the request’s outcome is available. With tail sampling, collectors buffer spans and choose once the result and duration are available. Tail sampling can retain rare failures, but every service still needs to generate and export its spans, and the collectors need enough memory for the decision window. Checkout used tail sampling, as configured in Listing Listing.

A trace is retained if any policy matches. Every error, slow request, pending or failed outcome, and retried payment is retained, along with 5 percent of all other traces, which give engineers normal requests to compare against. If about 3 percent of checkouts are slow or failed, the policy retains roughly 8 percent of traces and reduces stored trace data from about 200 GB to about 16 GB a day.

Each collector received about 600 new traces per second during peak traffic. A 15-second decision window could therefore buffer roughly 9,000 traces in memory. The num_traces limit allowed room for bursts, while the memory limiter protected the collector against large traces that consumed more memory than expected. If the collector began rejecting telemetry, that loss appeared in monitoring rather than being mistaken for evidence that requests had completed successfully.

Tail sampling across several collectors also requires every span of a trace to reach the same collector, because a collector can evaluate only a trace it has received in full. The agents make this happen by sending spans through the collector’s load-balancing exporter, with the trace identifier as the routing key. And because the policy retains every failed trace but only some successful ones, the trace store overstates the error rate. Service indicators must be calculated from metrics, which include every request.

SLIs, SLOs, and Outcome Accounting

Everything so far helps an engineer investigate a single incident, but the support ticket raises a bigger concern. How many other customers had the same experience without ever contacting support? Finding out needs measurements that run all the time. A service level indicator, or SLI, is the ratio of good events to eligible events, with both terms defined in writing, and a service level objective, or SLO, is the target for that ratio over a stated period. Expressing reliability as a ratio of events, rather than as average latency or uptime, ties it to what users experienced. It also lets a team work out how many bad events it can afford, which is the basis of the error budgets in the next section.

Response, Status, and Resolution SLIs

Indicators come from the user’s journey. A customer at checkout needs three things, a prompt response, a way to check on the operation if that response is lost, and a final outcome before the wait becomes unreasonable. Each of these can fail while the others still work, so checkout has three indicators. You will find the same three needs in almost any long-running user operation, from a bank transfer to a document upload.

Response indicator.

The fraction of eligible checkout requests for which the gateway returns a confirmation, a business rejection, or a pending response within 3 seconds. Target: 99 percent over 30 days.

Status indicator.

The fraction of authorized status requests for which the gateway returns the operation’s state, with HTTP status 200, within 1 second. The state may come from a cache and lag the committed state by up to 2 seconds, a limit checked separately by sampling. Target: 99.9 percent over 30 days.

Resolution indicator.

The fraction of accepted checkout operations that reach a final outcome (confirmed, rejected, or canceled) within 15 minutes of acceptance. Operations sent to manual risk review have their own 24-hour deadline. Target: 99.5 percent over 30 days.

The status target is the strictest, for two reasons. A status lookup is a simple read that does not depend on the provider, which makes high reliability achievable, and a failed lookup leaves the customer unsure whether they have paid. All three indicators are needed because each detects a failure the other two miss. A pending response returned within 3 seconds satisfies the response indicator even if the operation is then unresolved for an hour, which only the resolution indicator detects. Likewise, a status endpoint that fails while every operation resolves on time satisfies the resolution indicator, which only the status indicator detects.

Deciding which events are good takes judgment. A provider decline is a good response, because the customer receives a clear result. A generic “try again” page is not, because if the payment may already have gone through, that advice can lead the customer to pay twice. A pending response is good only if it tells the customer how to check on the order and its state was saved before the response was sent, because otherwise the customer receives a promise with nothing behind it.

Eligibility and Missing Completions

An indicator can detect only the failures its denominator includes. For the response indicator, eligible requests are authenticated, well-formed checkout submissions that reach the gateway, and capacity rejections, upstream failures, timeouts, and disconnections after acceptance are all treated as bad. Malformed requests are excluded, but their number appears on the dashboard so that a sudden increase is noticed.

Where events are recorded matters as much as which events are included. As the first section explained, the gateway runs outside the service’s process, so it records requests lost in a service crash that the service itself could never report. The gateway can also crash, however. Because checkout and status requests share the same gateway pool, requests lost that way have to be detected from outside. The team compares load-balancer request totals with gateway totals every minute, looks for browser submission reports with no gateway entry, and runs the external probes.

Coverage Gaps

Each of these measurements can fail silently, because a missing measurement and a healthy one both produce a quiet dashboard until something checks for the absence. Table Table lists how each measurement can fail and what detects the failure.

SLI Query Implementation

The response indicator comes from the gateway histogram, with the 3-second bucket providing the deadline and the outcome label identifying usable results, as shown in Listing Listing. The increase(…[30d]) function returns how much each counter increased over 30 days. Querying 30 days of raw histogram series is slow, though, so in practice hourly numerators and denominators are precalculated with recording rules and then summed.

The status indicator uses the same kind of histogram for the status route, status_request_duration_seconds, with a bucket at 1 second. It is measured from production customer requests rather than from probes, because a fault can affect only some operations, such as those with a corrupt cache entry, while a probe against its test order goes on succeeding.

An HTTP 200 response can still contain a stale or wrong state, so correctness is checked separately by sampling. Each status response includes the version of the state it returned, and a consistency checker examines 1 percent of responses. A sampled response is treated as correct when a transition with that version exists and records the same state, and when no newer transition was committed more than 2 seconds before the response was served, with both timestamps taken from clocks synchronized to the same time source. Comparing each response with the operation’s current state would be simpler, but the state may have changed legitimately after the response was sent, and every such change would then be flagged as an error. The mismatch rate has its own alert and is excluded from the status indicator, because a sample estimates correctness rather than measuring every response.

The resolution indicator cannot come from request metrics, because its deadline arrives long after the original request has ended, so a background evaluator calculates it instead. Every minute, the evaluator selects accepted operations whose deadline has passed, starting from the durable acceptance record introduced in Chapter 3, and looks up when each operation’s final outcome was first committed, because the current state alone would make a late resolution seem timely. It then writes one evaluation row per operation, keyed by the operation identifier so that two evaluator workers cannot record the same operation twice, and increments resolution_evaluations_total with a good or bad label. The evaluator also exports the number of operations waiting to be evaluated, because a stalled evaluator would otherwise stop producing bad events just when they matter most.

Error Budgets and Alerting

An SLO of 99.9 percent allows 0.1 percent of eligible events to be bad. That allowance, the error budget, turns reliability into something a team can spend, much like a monthly household budget. For one million status requests in 30 days, the budget is one thousand bad responses, shared by every source of bad events, from failed releases to dependency outages. When most of the budget has been used, the team slows down its releases, and when most of it is unspent, the team can accept more release risk.

To decide when to alert, you need to know how fast the budget is being spent. If you have spent half of your monthly budget by the fifth of the month, you do not need to wait until the end of the month to know something is wrong. That speed is the burn rate, the observed fraction of bad events divided by the allowed fraction. burn rate=observed bad-event fraction1−SLO target\text{burn rate} = \frac{\text{observed bad-event fraction}} {1-\text{SLO target}}burn rate=1−SLO targetobserved bad-event fraction​

If 1,300 of those million requests are bad, the burn rate is 0.13 percent divided by 0.1 percent, or 1.3. At that rate, the budget runs out after about 23 days instead of lasting the full 30. The window over which the burn rate is measured matters as much as the number itself, because a burn rate over five minutes describes what is happening now, whereas one over 30 days describes whether the objective will be met.

A paging threshold starts with a decision about how much budget the team is willing to lose before waking someone up. The platform team chose 2 percent of the 30-day budget in one hour. Because a 30-day window contains 720 hours, spending 2 percent in one hour corresponds to a burn rate of 0.02×720=14.40.02 \times 720 = 14.40.02×720=14.4. The alert in Listing Listing fires when the status burn rate exceeds 14.4 over both the last hour and the last five minutes, provided that the hour contains at least 500 requests.

The one-hour window makes sure that about 2 percent of the budget has been spent before anyone is paged, and the five-minute window makes sure that the problem is still happening, so the alert clears about five minutes after a fix. A fast-burn alert misses slow leaks, however. A service failing at twice its allowed rate never gets near 14.4, yet it uses up its budget in 15 days. A second alert opens a ticket when the burn rate exceeds 1 over both the last three days and the last six hours. This combination of long and short windows comes from Google’s Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) Workbook, and open-source tools such as Sloth and Pyrra can generate the recording and alerting rules for you from an SLO definition.

Low volume and missing data.

Ratios become unreliable when the denominator is small. With twenty status requests in an hour, a single failure is a 5 percent failure rate and a burn rate of 50, which is why the alert requires at least 500 requests in the hour. Below that volume, a separate rule opens a ticket after five bad requests in an hour and pages only if an external probe for the same endpoint is also failing. Missing data needs its own alert, because a ratio with an empty denominator has no value, and an alert expression with no value never fires. If the gateway stopped emitting metrics, every burn-rate alert would stop evaluating at the same moment. Separate alerts fire when checkout or status traffic drops to zero during hours that always have traffic, and when absent(status_request_duration_seconds_count) becomes true.

Routing.

A page should name the dashboard or runbook where the responder begins. Each customer-facing alert includes the affected region, the eligible and bad totals, recent deployment versions, and exemplar links to slow traces. Alertmanager groups related alerts, so forty failing instances produce one notification instead of forty, and it sends pages to the on-call engineer and component alerts to a ticket queue.

Measuring Release Impact

Baodium’s investigation found payment retries and connection waits on the critical path. The team released database connections before making the provider call, then compared acquisition delay and payment outcomes against the previous version during a canary. Connection waits fell without increasing unresolved payments. The release decision used both a resource measurement and the customer outcome indicator. Chapter 10 develops the canary population, thresholds, and observation window.

Testing Monitoring Coverage

Much of your instrumentation code runs only when something fails, which means it rarely runs at all, and a broken timeout handler or disconnect branch can go unnoticed for months. The only reliable way to confirm that a failure will be recorded correctly is to cause it on purpose in a staging environment and look at what the telemetry shows. Fire drills work the same way. You find out whether the alarms and exits work before there is an actual fire. The platform team runs five such tests on the checkout path.

Provider timeout.

A stub provider delays its first response past the attempt timeout. The payment span must show a timeout rather than a decline, the retry must carry the same operation reference, and the reconciliation trace must link back to the checkout trace.

Worker crash.

A worker is terminated immediately after writing the acceptance record, and the operation must still reach the resolution evaluator and be recorded as bad when its deadline passes.

Client disconnect.

A test client closes its connection one second into a checkout, and the gateway must record a disconnected outcome rather than a returned response.

Pool exhaustion.

The pool is reduced to one connection, which the test occupies, and the acquisition span must appear before any query span.

Unreadable status.

A committed operation’s cache entry is corrupted so that the status endpoint returns HTTP 500 for that operation alone. The status indicator must record every lookup of that operation as bad, even though the resolution indicator and the external probe report success.

Each test ends with automated queries against the monitoring backend, so it can run again after every instrumentation change. Two of the tests have already found production defects. The unreadable-status test showed why the status indicator must be measured from production requests. The pool-exhaustion test found a service whose database client created no acquisition span at all, so its time spent waiting for the pool had been reported as query time.

Field note

Facebook, October 2021

During maintenance on October 4, 2021, a command intended to assess the capacity of Facebook’s backbone network instead cut the connections between its data centers, and an audit tool that should have blocked the command failed because of a bug. Facebook’s DNS servers, which were designed to withdraw their Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) advertisements when they lost contact with the data centers, did just that, and the same loss of network access disabled many of the internal tools engineers would have used for repair. Engineers had to travel to the data centers in person before they could restore service.

Baodium’s telemetry pipeline depends on the same network and identity systems as checkout, so a failure in those systems would also take down the dashboards the on-call engineer relies on, leaving only the external probes to report. For each tool you would use to diagnose or recover from an outage, list what it depends on, and rehearse a recovery route that still works when that dependency is unavailable.

Asynchronous Document Processing SLIs

The same boundaries apply to work that finishes long after its request. Let’s consider a document-processing API that receives an upload, records a durable job, extracts searchable text, stores the result, and sends a completion notification. The HTTP request may finish in milliseconds while processing continues for minutes. Instrumenting it begins by asking, for each recorded event, which fact it proves. An accepted response establishes that the API took responsibility for the job under its documented contract. Worker completion establishes that one processing attempt reached its terminal step. A customer-visible result requires the durable output and any required index or retrieval contract to be available.

You need the same three vantage points as checkout. The edge records requests and responses, the workflow store records each job’s identity and state, and the delivery side records whether the customer could retrieve the result. A high rate of successful HTTP responses tells you uploads are being accepted, and a healthy consumer offset tells you workers are reading, but neither tells you a customer can find the processed document.

A useful trace tracks the request into the durable operation and correlates later worker attempts using a recorded operation ID. The ID may appear in restricted logs and trace attributes, with an access policy appropriate to the data. Using an operation ID as a Prometheus label would create a new time series for every operation. We can aggregate metrics by service, operation kind, outcome, and a bounded set of error categories, then use the operation store when an investigation requires individual unfinished operations.

For example, the processing SLI might be the fraction of accepted jobs that become retrievable within five minutes. Its denominator is all accepted jobs whose evaluation window has elapsed, including those that never started. The numerator requires an output verification record, not merely a successful worker exit. A second SLI can measure admission availability, and a third can measure the rate of unresolved or incorrect terminal states. Each SLI detects a failure the others miss.

Suppose a worker fails after uploading the object but before the index commit. The trace ends, the object exists, and yet the document never appears in search results. Recovery has to find that job and resume it from its recorded stage, and the only way it can is if the team decided, before release, which records would reveal a job stuck in that gap. Chapter 12 establishes the replay rules for its asynchronous stages, and Appendix A develops auditing when records in different sources conflict.

Summary

The customer’s question, “did it go through?”, is a good test for any monitoring setup. If your records cannot settle it for one specific request, the dashboards are measuring machine health while the service’s outcome is still unknown. This chapter asks you to measure the outcomes users experience, with component health as supporting evidence. A committed order, a response the gateway sent, and a confirmation the customer saw are three different facts, recorded in three different places, and the system needs a shared identifier that links them.

With that in place, the three kinds of telemetry each have a clear job. Metrics tell you which requests are affected and how many. Traces show where one request spent its time. Logs and durable records tell you what happened to a particular operation after the request ended. Service level indicators then measure what users experienced, with denominators that include the failures and alerts that fire when data goes missing. When you design the next feature, decide early which question an engineer will need to settle at three in the morning, and make sure some record can settle it.

Those measurements also show when demand exceeds what a shared resource can safely accept. Deciding what to do with that excess is the subject of Chapter 9.

Hidden assumptions

Assumption and scope & Component measurements below their paging thresholds mean that checkout is meeting its customer-facing commitments.
Condition that tests it & Requests complete without errors while responses are lost, status lookups fail for some operations, or operations are left unresolved.
Constraint or invariant & Committed state, returned responses, and displayed results are separate observations, and every indicator names its eligible events, point of measurement, and treatment of missing data.
Evidence and uncertainty & Traces and pool metrics separate connection waiting from connection occupancy, provider records establish how many authorizations occurred, and each known telemetry gap has a detection measurement.

Still unknown: how many display reports are lost in practice, and whether the telemetry pipeline is usable during a network or identity outage.
Signal and evaluation window & Burn rate for each indicator over the objective window and the fast-burn and slow-burn windows, with a minimum event volume and a missing-data alert.
Control and decision & Page on fast burn, open a ticket on slow burn or a failed component, and treat missing telemetry as an unresolved measurement problem.
Owner and review trigger & The checkout team owns outcome definitions and indicators, and the platform team owns the telemetry pipeline, health checks, and probes. Review after any incident in which requests appeared successful but the customer’s outcome was not, and before expanding a release.
